s: is_a gold coin [in rolls] The money is repeatedly placed on red, won, divided into three possible stakes, and finally gathered by Cecil and placed in the woman's care. It is packed into a heavy bag and taken with the couple to the train.

is_won_by Frenchman (the woman's husband) [at roulette] The woman says that the Frenchman has won half of the 20,000 francs, and Cecil later tells him that he has won more than 20,000 francs. The winnings are used to secure the couple's future rather than being risked again.

l: train to Paris, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Train to Paris departs Monte Carlo at midnight; Cecil boards a couple, buys tickets, and warns they are alone in a locked compartment until home.

l: departure for Paris, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: A departure for Paris follows successful roulette wagers and Cecil's decision to remove a Frenchman and his wife from Monte Carlo; they leave gratefully while Cecil remains alone on the platform.

l: homecoming to England, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_planned_by Cecil Harringford Cecil decides to take the first available train and return to England with Walters. He describes this homecoming as a return to England, Harringford, and his father.

l: happiness for the rest of their lives, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: A promise that a couple will be happy for the rest of their lives is voiced by the Frenchman, echoed by train wheels, linked by Cecil to his father’s letter, and repeated as he sleeps.

l: Miss Catherwaight's collection of dishonored honors, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Miss Catherwaight’s collection of dishonored honors is a collection of more than a hundred medals and decorations bought during travels with her father. Its items, including Legion of Honor crosses, English war medals, a Victoria Cross, and named gold and silver medals, had been awarded for service, virtue, bravery, statesmanship, or artistic genius, then pawned or sold by their recipients. She calls them second-hand honors and pledges to patriotism and pawnshops.

l: Lewis Lyman Lockwood, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Lewis Lyman Lockwood is an old, unmarried lawyer whose named medal is found and returned through Miss Catherwaight. The medal had been kept in his safe on Thirty-fifth Street before burglars robbed his home. Lockwood had been devoted friends with Henry Burgoyne from boyhood, but they quarrelled over a woman whom both loved; Lockwood also misunderstood the kindness of Miss Catherwaight’s mother, and pride sustained the separation. He lives with and serves as guardian to Mr. Latimer, whom he adopts in a manner. After Miss Catherwaight returns the medal, Lockwood thanks her, speaks with Burgoyne, and returns happier, announcing that the two will go shooting in Maryland.

l: Judge Burgoyne, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Judge Burgoyne, identified as Henry Burgoyne, is a judge and lawyer and the former boyhood friend of Lewis Lockwood. They attended school, roomed at State college, practiced law, and shared shooting, but became estranged after both loved the same woman. Later, Lockwood visits Burgoyne to see whether their long separation can end, and they plan a shooting trip in Maryland.

l: Mr. Latimer, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Mr. Latimer, a young man, is Lewis L. Lockwood’s junior law-office partner, adopted charge, and ward, as well as a dancing acquaintance of Miss Catherwaight. He tells her that Lockwood’s stolen silver medal marked Lockwood’s boyhood friendship with Henry Burgoyne, recounting the friends’ history and later quarrel. He accompanies Lockwood to visit Miss Catherwaight, waits for Lockwood’s return, notes Lockwood’s unused hunting preparations, and agrees to manage the office while Lockwood and Burgoyne travel.

l: the woman loved by Lockwood and Burgoyne, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Miss Catherwaight's mother, married to Mr. Catherwaight, was kind to Lewis L. Lockwood before her marriage; his misunderstanding of that kindness unwittingly caused trouble between Lockwood and Burgoyne.

l: Henry Burgoyne and Lewis L. Lockwood's boyhood friendship, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Henry Burgoyne and Lewis L. Lockwood's boyhood friendship begins at school in Westchester County, deepens as they room together at State college, and continues when they practise law as a firm in Tuckahoe. They share leisure, hunting, shooting, and loyalty, and are described as closer than brothers. The old, deeply valued bond ends when both love the same woman and each believes the other disloyal. Despite a long separation, the friendship survives, and Miss Catherwaight's intervention moves them toward reconciliation.

l: medals and decorations, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Medals and decorations are awarded for public service and high virtues such as bravery, statesmanship, and artistic genius. After recipients pawn or sell them, they enter Miss Catherwaight’s collection, including French crosses, English war medals, a Victoria Cross, and a congressional gold medal; she especially values discreditable histories.

l: silver heart medal from Henry Burgoyne to Lewis L. Lockwood, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: A cheap, tarnished silver heart medal, engraved with clasped hands and inscribed “From Henry Burgoyne to his beloved friend Lewis L. Lockwood” and “Through prosperity and adversity,” belongs to Lewis L. Lockwood as a keepsake. Stolen from his safe during a burglary, it is pawned and appears in the Bowery, where Miss Catherwaight buys or finds it in an old curiosity shop. After Mr. Latimer tells her its painful history, she refuses to keep or exhibit it and returns it to Lockwood. Though he first sees it as a reminder of the past, he keeps it at her urging.
is_the_destination_of Lockwood and Burgoyne's shooting trip [for a few weeks] Maryland is the destination of Lockwood and Burgoyne's planned shooting trip, which they intend to take for a few weeks.

l: the collection of dishonored honors, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The collection of dishonored honors is Miss Catherwaight's unusual hobby and consists of awards whose recipients have parted with them. She displays the objects to dinner guests and explains the circumstances of their sale or pawning, treating the contrast between public honor and private dishonor as the collection's chief interest. The silver heart medal prompts her to question whether every object should be treated as a collectible.

l: misunderstanding between Lockwood and Burgoyne, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: A long estrangement between Lewis L. Lockwood and Henry Burgoyne began when Lockwood misread Miss Catherwaight's mother's kindness and endured because both men's pride prevented reconciliation.

l: Lockwood and Burgoyne's shooting trip, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Lockwood visits Burgoyne, and they decide to take a shooting trip together to Maryland, planned to last a few weeks.

l: the three little girls from the East Side, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The three little girls from the East Side live on Hester Street with their mother and carry a lunch basket on an outing. In the Park, they watch the swan-boats and imagine lake sights. Unable to afford a ride, they are taken by Van Bibber, enjoy it, receive week-long tickets, and return to their tenement sunburned and delighted.

l: the Girl He Knew, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The Girl He Knew is a young lady known to Van Bibber who wears a riding-habit. On a hot day in the Park, she meets him at the dock after his ride with three little girls, smiles kindly, and invites him to join her and her brother at the stables.

l: the brother (the Girl He Knew's brother), Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_a brother [of the Girl He Knew] The brother meets Van Bibber at the lake after the swan-boat ride. He jokes about Van Bibber's trip and introduces the girls as Van Bibber's young lady friends from Hester Street, then teases the girls about smuggling laces and tipping the smoking-room steward.

l: the lake, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The lake is an artificial body of water in the Park, with a middle island, rocks, shallow edges, bushes, and narrow straits. Fish swim among its rocks, sparrows and robins bathe in its shallows, and girls imagine wild animals on the island.

l: the swan-boats, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The swan-boats are Lohengrin swans with paddle-wheel attachments that circle the lake beneath a parti-awning. Though Van Bibber first considers them idiotic, he later rides one with the girls and buys tickets for further trips.

l: the swan-boat ride, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: provides views of fishes and ducks [according to Eddie Case] The swan-boat ride is shady and pleasant, with the boat careening slightly as it turns. Van Bibber is embarrassed while other people can see him, but he relaxes in the narrow straits and helps the girls appreciate the sights.

l: riding the swan-boats, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Riding the swan-boats gives the three little girls great pleasure, and Van Bibber finds that they seem to enjoy it more than he has enjoyed expensive trips by yacht or steamship. Afterward, the girls use the tickets Van Bibber gives them until they are sunburned.

l: Van Bibber's generosity, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: benefits the three little girls from the East Side [by providing tickets] Van Bibber's generosity leads him to pay for the three little girls' swan-boat ride when they cannot afford it. He later buys each girl a long string of tickets so they can continue riding for a week.

A gentleman of the press experienced throughout New York at all hours, he regards city reporters’ work as commonplace and repetitive, with dramas rooted in crime, poverty, or drink rather than mystery. While accompanying Van Bibber to a Jersey City prizefight, he argues this view, recounts a Dickens story, and another reporter keeps time.

The burglar is a recently released prisoner who has served seven years in prison. Escaping with a revolver and bags of stolen goods, he is overpowered by Van Bibber after emerging beside a great house. He refuses to return to prison alive and says he stole money to reach his wife, living in the West under another name, and his daughter, who does not know him. Van Bibber sends him to Helena, Montana, where he seeks an honest living with them.

l: Abe Hubbard, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Abe Hubbard, also known as Jimmie the Gent, is an escaped burglar traced to New York. A newspaper identifies him as the burglar whom Van Bibber helped after Van Bibber went to Jersey City to see a fight.

l: Jimmie the Gent, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: has_alias Abe Hubbard The newspaper identifies Abe Hubbard by the alias Jimmie the Gent and reports that he has broken jail.

l: Helena, Montana, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Helena, Montana, is the destination the burglar gives when Van Bibber asks where he should send him. Van Bibber buys the burglar a train ticket to Helena, Montana.

l: the burglary of the great house, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: is_committed_by burglar The burglary is discovered when Van Bibber sees a man carrying two bags filled with projecting articles near the great house. He assumes the man has robbed the house and makes him leave the bags inside the kitchen door, where a servant can find them.

l: Abe Hubbard's jail break, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Abe Hubbard, alias Jimmie the Gent, breaks jail in New Jersey and is traced to New York. A newspaper says detectives expect to recapture him, but fear his friends may help him escape out West.

is_described_as grave [by the burglar] The burglar says he has served his time in prison and describes returning there as returning to a grave. He claims he spent seven years imprisoned and fears another sentence of twenty years.

The burglar carries a revolver during the attempted escape. It goes off once during his struggle with Van Bibber, who kicks it from his hand and keeps it as a threat while escorting him to the station.

l: stolen bags, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Two bags containing articles of different sizes lie at the burglar's feet. Van Bibber tells him to place the bags inside the kitchen door, where the servant will see them before the milkman does.

l: train ticket, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: destination Helena, Montana Van Bibber buys the burglar a ticket to Helena, Montana. He warns that the ticket can be sold downtown for half its value, and the burglar says he already knows that.

Van Bibber wants to prove the reporter wrong about the absence of unusual adventures in city life. His encounter with the burglar becomes the extraordinary incident he has been seeking, though he later wonders whether he acted correctly.

l: honest living, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The burglar says he intended to live honestly after joining his wife and daughter in the West. Van Bibber doubts whether the burglar truly means to live honestly but nevertheless gives him money and helps him leave.

l: young Standish, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Young Standish, or Ted, is the younger son of the Standish family and brother of elder Standish. He elopes with Miss Cambridge and seeks a clergyman to marry them before returning to Boston. When his older brother arrives, Van Bibber deceives him to protect the couple and arranges their public marriage.

l: Miss Cambridge, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: Miss Cambridge is a very young, very pretty lady who elopes with young Standish. Frightened because they lack a clergyman, witnesses, and parish registry, she relies on Van Bibber to arrange a formal wedding. Though she weeps on the journey, she smiles happily as she walks up the aisle.

l: Little Church Around the Corner, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The Little Church Around the Corner is a church with an old rector and assistant organist. It hosts the marriage ceremony of young Standish and Miss Cambridge at three o’clock after Van Bibber secures the rector, opening, music, and bell arrangements.

l: the wedding, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The wedding of Miss Cambridge and young Standish, called Ted, is properly and publicly arranged by Cortlandt Van Bibber at Little Church Around the Corner. To give their elopement publicity and prevent scandal, Van Bibber stages an orthodox, fashionable ceremony with prominent club-men witnesses, invited women, flowers, organ music, bell, rice, and an old shoe.

l: the elopement, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: The elopement concerns young Standish and Miss Cambridge, who leave without family approval or presence. With no clergyman or witnesses, Van Bibber protects them from discovery and, as best man, turns their hurried plan into a formal wedding.

l: marriage ceremony, Gallegher and Other Stories
s: takes_place_at Little Church Around the Corner [public and witnessed] The marriage ceremony takes place at the Little Church Around the Corner with an assistant organist, witnesses, and guests arranged by Van Bibber. Young Standish and Miss Cambridge are married there and then leave for the Fall River boat.

s: the second volume foreshadows the third volume (through its change in manner)
q: The change, so extraordinary in the third volume, is foreshadowed in the second.

s: Schummel’s self-criticism describes the ninety-page autobiography (as ill conceived and incoherent)
q: he confesses that the ninety-page autobiography which precedes the journey itself was intended to be Tristram-like, but openly stigmatizes his own failure as “ill conceived, incoherent and not very well told!”

s: Schummel’s self-criticism attributes the narrative (principally to Fielding and Richardson rather than Sterne)
q: he is also discerning in his assertion that the narrative contained in his volume is conceived more in the vein of Fielding and Richardson.

s: Johann Wolfgang Goethe compares Die Grosse Begebenheit aus kleinen Ursachen (to a thistle found on Yorick’s grave)
q: Goethe calls the book a thistle which he has found on Yorick’s grave.

s: Goethe’s review of the second volume condemns Schummel (as a childish imitator)
q: Schummel is stigmatized as a childish imitator and his book is censured as “beneath criticism,”

s: Sterne’s peculiar genius is appreciated by Schummel (despite Schummel’s inability to follow Yorick fully)
q: The awkwardness with which this is done proves Schummel’s inability to follow Yorick, though its use shows his appreciation of Sterne’s peculiar genius.

s: Shandean narration and stylistic devices includes the black margin to pages 199-206, the line upside down (p. 175), the twelve irregularly printed lines (p. 331) (Shandean)
q: Shandean also is the black margin to pages 199-206, the line upside down (p. 175), the twelve irregularly printed lines (p. 331)

s: Empfindsamkeit is expressed in the episode of vicarious begging (as a highly sentimental idea)
q: introducing the new and highly sentimental idea of “vicarious begging” (pp. 268-9).

s: Tristram Shandy influences Die Grosse Begebenheit aus kleinen Ursachen (through its narrator’s frankness about parental eccentricities)
q: the suggestion is given that this feature was derived from Tristram’s own frankness concerning the eccentricities and incapacities of his parents.

s: the second volume contains the story of the rescued baker’s wife (in a purely sentimental and effusive manner)
q: Purely sentimental, effusive, and abundantly teary is the story of the rescued baker’s wife.
